query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing continuous in-situ ultrasonic vibration (20–40 kHz, 3–15 µm amplitude) to the build plate during laser-powder-bed-fusion (LPBF) of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy-alloy (HEA) parts will (a) cut average dimensional deviation from the CAD model by ≈30 % and (b) raise room-temperature yield strength by ≈10 %, while halving lack-of-fusion porosity compared with an otherwise identical LPBF process run without vibration.
generation.material_initial_state: Gas-atomised CoCrFeMnNi HEA powder, 15–45 µm, spherical morphology; stainless steel build plate; standard LPBF machine under flowing Ar; preheat 200 °C.
generation.intervention: Apply longitudinal ultrasonic vibration to the build plate throughout powder spreading and laser exposure (frequency 20–40 kHz, peak-to-peak amplitude 3–15 µm).
generation.conditions: Layer thickness 30 µm; laser power 200 W; scan speed 800 mm s⁻¹; hatch spacing 80 µm; argon atmosphere <100 ppm O₂; build envelope 200 °C; vibration on continuously from first layer to final layer.
generation.structural_mediator: Finer, more equiaxed FCC grains (~1–3 µm) and >99.5 % relative density versus ~25 µm columnar grains and 98 % density in the baseline.
generation.mechanism: Ultrasonic vibration improves powder packing density and wetting, induces acoustic streaming and cavitation in the melt pool, breaks dendrite arms, and homogenises temperature fields; the combined effects (1) suppress lack-of-fusion pores and keyhole instability, (2) refine grains by increasing heterogeneous nucleation sites, and (3) lower residual stress and distortion, yielding tighter dimensional tolerances and higher strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with baseline LPBF with no vibration: 1. Dimensional precision: mean absolute deviation from CAD reduced from 120 µm to ≤85 µm (≈30 %). 2. Mechanical integrity: 0.2 % proof stress rises from 720 MPa to ≥790 MPa (≈10 %). 3. Internal defects: lack-of-fusion porosity fraction drops from 2 vol % to ≤1 vol % (≈50 % decrease).
generation.baseline: Identical LPBF build parameters but with the vibration generator turned off.
generation.boundary: Effect expected for FCC HEAs with liquidus 1550–1650 °C processed by LPBF under 150–250 W laser power and layer thickness ≤50 µm. Outside 3–15 µm amplitude or >50 kHz, powder spatter and noise dominate and benefits diminish.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of grain refinement and the trade-off between vibration-induced spatter versus densification remain uncertain; scaling to large parts may attenuate the acoustic field.

falsification_experiment.design: Print 30 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm tensile coupons and 20 mm cubes in a commercial LPBF machine under the stated conditions, half with vibration OFF (control) and half with vibration ON (test). Maintain identical thermal histories otherwise.
measurements: 3-D optical scanning of cubes for dimensional deviation
X-ray µCT for porosity volume fraction and pore morphology
Electron backscatter diffraction for grain size and texture
Room-temperature tensile tests for 0.2 % yield strength
Residual stress via X-ray diffraction depth profiling
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the vibration-ON samples do NOT show simultaneously (i) ≥20 % reduction in dimensional deviation, (ii) ≥5 % increase in yield strength, and (iii) ≥25 % reduction in porosity relative to vibration-OFF controls, the hypothesis is falsified.
